subject: Scam Alert #1: the IRS isn't texting you
preheader: Tax season's fakes are out. 1 rule beats all of them.
html:
Tax season's fakes are out. 1 rule beats all of them.

Hi,

Welcome to the first weekly Scam Alert: one scam, decoded, every Thursday. It's tax season, so the fake IRS is everywhere this week.

This week's scam: "verify your IRS account"

Spotted this week (fictional example): "IRS: Your online account has been suspended. Verify your identity within 24 hours to release your refund: [link]"

The link opens a perfect copy of the IRS sign-in page. It takes your login, then asks for a photo of your driver's license "to confirm it's you." With both, someone can file a return in your name or get into your real account.

The tell

The IRS doesn't text or email you out of the blue about refunds or your account. So any message like this is fake, however official it looks.

What to do

  1. Delete the link. To check your real account, type IRS.gov yourself.
  2. Already entered your details? Change that password now, and follow the steps at IRS.gov's identity theft page.
  3. Forward the text to 7726 (the free spam-reporting number), then report it at IRS.gov.

Quick hits

  • The arrest call: "There's a warrant, pay today with gift cards." The real IRS doesn't threaten arrest or demand a payment method. Hang up and report it at tigta.gov.
  • State refund texts: scammers copy your state's tax department too. Check your refund on your state's official .gov site.
  • Free tool: an IRS Identity Protection PIN stops anyone else filing a return with your Social Security number.

Your 5-minute job this week

Get your IRS Identity Protection PIN. Search "IRS IP PIN" and make sure the address is irs.gov, or go there directly. It's free, and it's one of the best anti-fraud tools the IRS has.

subject: Scam Alert #2: "send me a photo of the back of the card"
preheader: Valentine's week scams, and one conversation worth having with your teen.
html:
Valentine's week scams, and one conversation worth having with your teen.

Hi,

Valentine's Day is Sunday, which makes this one of the busiest weeks of the year for romance scammers. And Tuesday was Safer Internet Day, so there's one more conversation at the end worth having.

This week's scam: the gift card favor

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Babe I'm so embarrassed to ask. My card isn't working out here and I wanted to send you something for Valentine's. Could you grab 3 gift cards and send me a photo of the backs? I'll pay you back the second I'm home 💕"

After weeks of good-morning texts, it feels small. But that photo is the money: the number and PIN let them spend it in seconds, and it's almost impossible to get back.

The tell

Anyone you've only met online who asks for gift cards is a scammer. The FTC is clear on this. No exceptions, however real they feel.

What to do

  1. Say it kindly, once: "I don't send money or gift cards to anyone I haven't met in person. Let's video chat this week."
  2. Already sent one? Call the gift card company on the number on the card, right away, and keep the receipt.
  3. Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

Quick hits

  • "Your Valentine's gift couldn't be delivered": a $1.99 "redelivery fee" text is after your card number. Ask the sender, or check the carrier's own app.
  • The deployed soldier: if an online partner "needs" $2,500 for leave papers, it's a scam. The US Army says soldiers don't pay to go on leave.
  • The package stuck in customs: if they "shipped you something" and a courier wants fees, there is no package.

Your 5-minute job this week

Send one message to a teen in your life: "If anyone online ever threatens you with a photo, come to me. I won't be angry, and we'll fix it together." Criminals who run sextortion count on kids being too scared to tell anyone. The FBI says don't pay, save the messages and report it. For under-18s, NCMEC's free Take It Down tool helps get images removed. If anyone feels unsafe, call or text 988.

Forward this to one person dating online right now.

The Scam Decoded team

P.S. Know someone whose online partner "keeps sending them things"? Forward them this issue, with no lecture attached.

subject: Scam Alert #3: a refund you didn't expect (and a call to "send it back")
preheader: Why a scammer would send YOU money, and what to do instead.
html:
Why a scammer would send YOU money, and what to do instead.

Hi,

This week's scam is backwards: it starts with someone sending you money.

This week's scam: the "send it back" refund

Spotted this week (fictional example): A $3,140 deposit labeled "IRS TREAS 310 TAX REF" lands in your account. Two days later a caller says: "That refund was issued in error. Return it to our collection partner today or you'll face penalties."

Someone used your stolen details to file a fake return, and the refund went to your real bank account. If you "send it back" where they say, the money's gone and you still owe the IRS.

The tell

The IRS doesn't call to demand you send a refund to a third party. A refund you didn't file for is a sign someone filed in your name.

What to do

  1. Don't send money anywhere a caller, email or letter tells you to.
  2. Call your bank, and follow the IRS's own steps for returning an erroneous refund (IRS Tax Topic 161 on IRS.gov).
  3. Report identity theft through IRS.gov, freeze your credit, and get an IP PIN for next year.

Quick hits

  • "Settle your tax debt for pennies on the dollar": the FTC warns some tax relief companies charge big fees up front. Check IRS payment plans and the free Taxpayer Advocate Service first.
  • Your tax software is stuck? Don't call a number from a search result. Use the help button inside the software.
  • Real IRS letters have a notice number in the corner. Look it up on IRS.gov's "understanding your notice" page.

Your 5-minute job this week

Sign in to your IRS online account (type IRS.gov yourself) and look around. Knowing what your real account looks like makes the fakes easier to spot.

Forward this to whoever does the taxes in your family.

The Scam Decoded team

P.S. Owe the IRS and feeling stressed about it? You're not alone. We made a calm video about the free options on our YouTube channel this Sunday.

subject: Scam Alert #4: "Hi Mom, this is my new number"
preheader: 6 texts from hello to a $1,900 bill, and the 2-minute fix.
html:
6 texts from hello to a $1,900 bill, and the 2-minute fix.

Hi,

This one goes to parents more than anyone, so if you're the adult child, forward it up the family tree.

This week's scam: the new number text

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Hi Mom, dropped my phone in the sink 🙄 this is my new number, save it and delete the old one x" ... (small talk) ... "Are you free? I have a bill due today and I can't log into my banking on this phone. Could you pay it and I'll send it back tomorrow?"

Every step is believable on its own. Phones break, bills are due. And "delete the old number" stops you calling the real one.

The tell

A new number, plus an urgent payment, plus "I can't talk right now." That combination is the scam.

What to do

  1. Call the old number anyway. It almost always still works.
  2. Or ask a question only your child would know, or use your family safe word.
  3. If it really is them, they can wait five minutes. Real family always can.

Quick hits

  • "Unpaid tax on your payment app transactions": real 1099-K forms come from the app itself. Tax is paid through IRS.gov, never a text link.
  • AI voice clones: the same scam now comes as a phone call that sounds like your child. A safe word beats it too.
  • The QR code in a package you didn't order: don't scan it. You can keep the item.

Your 5-minute job this week

Pick a family safe word tonight: something silly and memorable, never posted online. Text it to your family group in person or by phone call, not in a group chat that could be hacked. Anyone asking for money in a hurry has to say it.

subject: Scam Alert #5: Social Security numbers don't get "suspended"
preheader: Slam the Scam Day: 6 government imposters and the one rule that beats them.
html:
Slam the Scam Day: 6 government imposters and the one rule that beats them.

Hi,

Today is Slam the Scam Day, run by Social Security's inspector general to fight government imposter scams. (Check ssa.gov for the confirmed date each year.) So this issue is a field guide.

This week's scam: "your Social Security number has been suspended"

Spotted this week (fictional example): "This is the Social Security Administration. Your Social Security number has been suspended due to suspicious activity in Texas. Press 1 to speak to an officer."

The "officer" says your number was used in a crime, and the only way to protect your savings is to move them to a "safe account" today.

The tell

Social Security numbers don't get suspended. And no real agency will ever tell you to move your money to protect it.

What to do

  1. Hang up. If you're worried, call Social Security on the number from its official website.
  2. Never move money, buy gift cards or hand cash to a courier because of a call.
  3. Report it at oig.ssa.gov.

Quick hits: what the real agencies won't do

  • IRS: won't threaten arrest or demand gift cards. It usually starts with a letter.
  • Medicare: won't call asking for your Medicare number. Cards are free.
  • Courts: don't call to collect fines for missed jury duty.
  • The FTC: won't call to "protect your money" or say you're under investigation.
  • Your utility: won't demand gift cards, crypto or a store barcode to stop a shutoff.

Your 5-minute job this week

Agree on one family rule: we never pay anyone who called, texted or emailed us first. We hang up and call the real number ourselves. Then practice one line with your parents: "I don't do that on the phone. I'll call you back."

From Scam Decoded

The Family Scam-Proofing Kit has a fridge card with these rules in big type ($9, our own product).

Forward this to your parents for Slam the Scam Day.

The Scam Decoded team

P.S. If a parent tells you they got one of these calls, say "I'm glad you told me" before anything else. It's the line that makes them tell you next time.

subject: Scam Alert #6: the half-price beach house
preheader: Spring break rentals, March Madness "sure wins", and the one way to pay for travel.
html:
Spring break rentals, March Madness "sure wins", and the one way to pay for travel.

Hi,

Spring break and March Madness land in the same week, and so do two scams that look like great deals.

This week's scam: the fake vacation rental

Spotted this week (fictional example): "Hi! The beach house is still free for spring break 😊 If you book directly with me instead of through the site I can take off the fees, just send the $600 deposit by Zelle today, I have two other families asking."

The photos are often copied from a real listing. Once you pay off the platform, there's no protection, and the house might belong to someone else entirely.

The tell

A host who wants you off the booking site and paying by payment app, wire, gift card or crypto. The FTC flags all four.

What to do

  1. Reverse search the listing photos and look up the address on a map.
  2. Keep every message on the booking platform.
  3. Pay only through the platform or with a credit card, which gives you dispute rights if it turns out to be fake.

Quick hits

  • "Sure-win" March Madness picks: nobody can promise wins. If a betting app wants a fee before you can withdraw, the winnings were never real.
  • "Your power will be cut off in 30 minutes": hang up and call the number on your bill. Small businesses get this one a lot.
  • Spring clean your passwords: reused passwords are how one breach becomes five hacked accounts. A password manager fixes that.

Your 5-minute job this week

Turn on two-step sign-in for your email account. It's the key that resets every other password you have, so it's the one to lock first.
